## 1 Introduction to accounting and finance

**Tasks beside the method:** [Open this chapter’s tasks + hints](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/Tasks/Book%20chapter%201) · [Reading, home and tutoring routes](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/Practice).

### 1.1 Financial accounting and management accounting

| Area | Main purpose | Example question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Financial accounting | Report the business's position and performance, especially to external users | What does the business own and owe? |
| Management accounting | Help managers plan, control and choose actions | Should we accept this extra order? |
| Finance | Evaluate funding and investment over time | Is the future return worth the initial investment? |

The same event can matter in all three areas. Buying a machine creates an asset, influences product costs, and commits cash to an investment. Different questions require different ways of analysing it.

Useful information must be relevant to the decision and faithfully represent what happened. Comparability, understandable presentation, timely reporting and the ability to check the information also matter. Precise-looking numbers can still be poor information when the assumptions are wrong.

### 1.2 Useful information: qualities and users

Accounting is an information service. Owners assess returns and stewardship; lenders assess repayment and interest; managers plan and control; suppliers assess payment risk; employees, customers and public authorities have other decisions. A general-purpose financial statement can also be useful internally: financial accounting is not restricted to external readers.

| Quality | Meaning | Application |
|---|---|---|
| **Relevance** | Can influence a decision through predictive or confirmatory value | A product's avoidable cost matters to a closure decision |
| **Faithful representation** | Describes the economic substance; aims to be complete, neutral and free from error | Describe an uncertain estimate and its method rather than presenting invented certainty |
| Comparability | Like items treated alike; differences identifiable | Compare years after checking accounting-policy changes |
| Verifiability | Independent informed observers can broadly agree on the portrayal | Reconcile records and inspect assumptions |
| Timeliness | Arrives while it can affect the decision | A late forecast may no longer help |
| Understandability | Clearly organised for a reasonably informed reader | Define terms and separate subtotals |

The first two are the fundamental qualities. Enhancing qualities cannot rescue irrelevant or misleading information. **Materiality** concerns whether omission or misstatement could affect the decision; significance depends on nature and context as well as amount. “Free from error” does not make uncertain estimates perfectly predictable. The estimate, method and uncertainty must be properly described.

### 1.3 The business objective and the cost of information

The textbook's working financial objective is to enhance **owners' wealth**. Sales growth is not sufficient if costs grow faster. A positive accounting profit is not sufficient if invested capital earns less than its required return. NPV later measures value created after charging for timing and the opportunity cost of capital.

This financial objective does not remove obligations to employees, customers or other stakeholders. Long-run value depends on those relationships, risk and ethical reporting. An accountant should not manipulate estimates or omit material information to create a preferred impression.

An information system identifies events, records them, analyses them and communicates results. More detail is worthwhile only when its decision benefit justifies its cost. The reporting supplement gives a specific financing example of that principle.

### 1.4 Reliable reporting and the outside ownership share

An entrepreneur invests internal equity $EQ$ in a project costing $I$. The funding gap is $G=I-EQ$. New investors demand a share $\alpha$ of the project's value sufficient to cover $G$. The simplified teaching model uses competitive, risk-neutral valuation at one common valuation basis; do not apply its undiscounted expressions to a separate multi-year cash-flow problem.

If the high value $H$ is credibly revealed, $\alpha_H=G/H$. Without revelation, investors use $V(p)=pH+(1-p)L$ and demand $\alpha_p=G/V(p)$. The entrepreneur knows the project is high type. The value of avoiding excessive dilution is:

$$
B=(\alpha_p-\alpha_H)H.
$$

Here $p$ is the probability of a high project value, not the selling price used in later chapters; $L$ is the low project value, not liabilities; $0<p<1$, $H>L>I$ in the supplied model. Reporting must be credible; merely claiming “high value” does not reveal the type. Reporting costs are evaluated against the gross benefit under the model's assumption that they do not change the required investment or values.

| Supplied Chapter 1 assignment | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---:|
| Funding gap | £10m − £5m | £5m |
| High type revealed | £5m / £15m | 33.3333% ownership |
| Expected value without report | 0.2 × £15m + 0.8 × £11m | £11.8m |
| Outside share without report | £5m / £11.8m | 42.3729% |
| Gross benefit to high-type owner | (£5m / £11.8m − 1/3) × £15m | **£1,355,932.20** |

The benefit is before producing or auditing the report. At an equal reporting cost the owner is indifferent; above it, reporting destroys value under these assumptions. Increasing the probability of a high type makes the pooled valuation closer to $H$ and reduces the high-type owner's benefit from revealing information, holding other inputs fixed.

**Sources:** [Chapter 1 slides](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/sources/118859.pdf%23page%3D7); [reporting model](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/sources/132533.pdf%23page%3D1); [home assignment](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/sources/132527.pdf%23page%3D1); [book: qualities](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/sources/textbook-12e.pdf%23page%3D20); [book: wealth objective](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/sources/textbook-12e.pdf%23page%3D30).

## 2 Measuring and reporting financial position

**Tasks beside the method:** [Open this chapter’s tasks + hints](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/Tasks/Book%20chapter%202) · [Reading, home and tutoring routes](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/Practice).

### 2.1 Resources and claims

| Term | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Asset | A resource controlled by the business with potential future economic benefits | Cash, inventory, a van, a customer's unpaid bill |
| Liability | An obligation to another party | A supplier's unpaid invoice or a bank loan |
| Equity | Owners' residual interest after liabilities | Assets £12,000 − liabilities £4,000 = equity £8,000 |
| Revenue | Income earned from ordinary trading activities | Goods supplied to a customer for £500 |
| Expense | Resources consumed in earning the period's revenue | The cost of goods sold, rent used, depreciation |

**Inventory** means goods still held; **trade receivables** are amounts customers owe us; **trade payables** are amounts we owe suppliers. Receivables are assets because we expect collection. Payables are liabilities because we must settle them.

### 2.2 Three statements, three time perspectives

| Statement | Measures | Time perspective |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Statement of financial position / balance sheet | Assets, liabilities and equity | **At** a date: a snapshot |
| Income statement / profit and loss | Revenue, expenses and profit | **For** a period: performance |
| Statement of cash flows | Cash inflows and outflows | **For** a period: movement in cash |

**Assets = Equity + Liabilities.** Every transaction must preserve this relationship. Equity is a claim on net assets, rather than a separate pot of cash.

**Closing equity = opening equity + owner contributions + profit − owner distributions**, assuming no other equity movements. A loss reduces equity. Owner contributions increase equity without creating revenue; distributions reduce equity without being operating expenses.

**Remember:** position is what remains; profit is what was earned; cash flow is what moved. A profitable credit sale can increase receivables while bringing in no cash yet.

![statement-links](./static-data/vault-assets/EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/assets/statement-links.svg)

*Position is a stock at a date. Profit and cash flows measure different changes over a period; owner and financing transactions also matter.*

### 2.3 Classify before calculating

| Category | Typical items | Recognition cue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Non-current assets | Equipment, vehicles, buildings, some intangible resources | Used to provide benefits over the longer term |
| Current assets | Inventory, trade receivables, prepayments, cash | Used, sold or collected in the operating cycle or near term |
| Equity | Owner capital and retained profit | Owners' residual claim |
| Non-current liabilities | Longer-term borrowings | Settlement falls beyond the current category |
| Current liabilities | Trade payables, accrued expenses, short-term debt | Settlement expected in the operating cycle or near term |

The course uses the operating cycle and a one-year reference in classifying current items. Read repayment terms: a loan's current instalment can belong in current liabilities even when the rest is long term.

Buying an asset on credit creates **both** an asset and a liability. Settling that bill later removes cash and the liability; it does not create the asset for a second time.

### 2.4 A reusable statement layout

This is the final balance sheet from the connected teaching example used across Chapters 2, 3, DEB and 5, after one month's rent and depreciation adjustments.

| Statement of financial position at month-end | £ |
| --- | --- |
| **Non-current assets** | |
| Equipment: cost £3,000 less accumulated depreciation £50 | 2,950 |
| **Current assets** | |
| Inventory | 800 |
| Trade receivables | 500 |
| Prepaid rent | 600 |
| Cash at bank | 7,100 |
| **Total assets** | **11,950** |
| **Equity** | |
| Owner capital £10,000 + retained profit £450 | 10,450 |
| **Current liabilities** | |
| Trade payables | 1,500 |
| **Total equity and liabilities** | **11,950** |

**Method:** establish the reporting date → update every account → make period-end adjustments → group the closing balances → total both sides. Show a heading and date, distinguish subtotals, and make the two final totals easy to compare.

### 2.5 Conventions behind the numbers

| Convention | Practical meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Business entity | Keep the business's records separate from the owner's private spending |
| Historical cost | Begin with acquisition cost under the course's cost-based examples |
| Going concern | Prepare on the basis that the business continues, unless evidence indicates otherwise |
| Dual aspect | Record the connected effects of each transaction |
| Accruals and matching | Attribute revenue and consumed resources to the appropriate period |
| Consistency and prudence | Apply methods consistently and exercise caution over uncertain estimates |

A balance sheet is not a complete market valuation. Some resources are difficult to measure; carrying amounts depend on acquisition dates, estimates and accounting methods. A balanced statement confirms arithmetic consistency, rather than proving that every judgement is correct.

### 2.6 Recognition, useful lives and interpretation

A useful resource is not automatically a recognised asset. The course looks for a controlled resource arising from past events, with future benefit and a sufficiently reliable monetary measure under its recognition conventions. Skilled employees and internally built reputation can be valuable without appearing as purchased assets. A tangible asset has physical substance; an intangible asset does not.

Finite-life non-current assets are consumed over several periods: depreciation or amortisation allocates their depreciable cost. An **indefinite** life is not a promise of literal immortality; it means no foreseeable limit can be determined. The course's land and indefinite-life examples are not routinely depreciated, but may still lose recoverable value. Current assets are used, realised or consumed in the operating cycle or near term; the long-run useful-life classification is not the useful organising principle for them.

Read a financial-position statement for liquidity, financing mix and the resources available to generate returns. Compare dates and context: a year-end snapshot can hide seasonal stress, and historical carrying amounts are not necessarily market values. A short-term asset surplus does not prove receivables are collectible or inventory saleable.

With no other equity movements:

$$
E_1=E_0+K+\pi-D
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\pi=E_1-E_0-K+D.
$$

For opening equity £40,000, closing £54,000, contributions £6,000 and drawings £9,000, profit is £17,000. Contributions and drawings change equity without being revenue or operating expenses. The shortcut $\Delta E=\pi$ works only when there are no other equity movements.

## 3 Measuring and reporting financial performance

**Tasks beside the method:** [Open this chapter’s tasks + hints](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/Tasks/Book%20chapter%203) · [Reading, home and tutoring routes](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/Practice).

### 3.1 Build the income statement in layers

| Calculation | Meaning | Connected example £ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sales revenue | Value earned from supplying goods/services | 2,000 |
| Less cost of sales | Cost of inventory actually sold | (1,200) |
| **Gross profit** | Trading surplus before other operating expenses | **800** |
| Less rent expense | Rent consumed this month | (300) |
| Less depreciation | Equipment benefits consumed this month | (50) |
| **Operating profit** | Profit from operations | **450** |
| Non-operating items, interest and tax | Include separately when given | 0 |
| **Profit for the period** | Amount flowing into retained profit | **450** |

Gross profit and contribution (Chapter 7) measure different things. Cost of sales can contain both fixed and variable production costs; contribution subtracts variable costs relevant to the activity.

### 3.2 Inventory purchases and cost of sales

For a simple trading business, **cost of sales = opening inventory + purchases − closing inventory**, using comparable cost values and incorporating returns or other adjustments when given.

In the example, opening inventory is zero, purchases are £2,000 and closing inventory is £800. Therefore cost of sales = £0 + £2,000 − £800 = **£1,200**. The unsold £800 remains an asset because its benefits have not yet been consumed through sale.

### 3.3 Separate earning, collecting, buying and paying

| Event | Profit effect now | Cash effect now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Supply goods on credit | Revenue, and cost of the goods sold | None |
| Collect an existing receivable | No new revenue | Cash increases |
| Buy unsold inventory for cash | Normally no immediate cost-of-sales expense | Cash decreases |
| Repay a supplier for an earlier purchase | No second expense | Cash decreases |
| Receive a loan | No revenue | Cash increases |
| Repay loan principal | No operating expense | Cash decreases |

Revenue recognition depends on supplying the promised goods or services under the exercise's facts. An advance from a customer before performance normally creates an obligation to deliver, rather than immediate earned revenue. For work supplied over time, recognise the appropriate period's performance using the measure specified in the question.

### 3.4 Accrued expenses and prepayments

$$\text{Expense}=\text{cash paid}+\Delta\text{accrual}-\Delta\text{prepayment}.$$

Each change is closing minus opening: a higher accrual adds expense; a higher prepayment removes future benefits from the current expense.

| Situation | Income statement | Balance sheet | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Expense incurred but unpaid | Recognise the expense | Accrued liability | £200 electricity used but not paid |
| Paid for a future period | Recognise only the part consumed | Prepayment asset for the unused part | £900 for three months: £300 used, £600 prepaid |
| Revenue earned but uncollected | Recognise earned revenue | Receivable | Work completed for £500 on credit |
| Cash received before earning it | Recognise revenue as performance occurs | Liability for the unearned part | Customer advance for next month's service |

For an expense category, **expense = cash paid + closing accrual − opening accrual + opening prepayment − closing prepayment**, assuming no other movements. Beginning and ending balances matter: do not adjust only for the closing figures if opening balances are supplied.

In the rent example, £900 paid − £600 closing prepayment = **£300 expense**. Charging all £900 this month would understate both profit and the prepayment asset by £600.

### 3.5 Depreciation, carrying amount and impairment

| Method / term | Formula or meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Straight-line depreciation | (Cost − residual value) ÷ useful life | (£3,000 − £0) ÷ 5 years = £600 a year |
| Monthly straight-line amount | Annual charge ÷ 12, for equal months | £600 ÷ 12 = £50 |
| Reducing-balance depreciation | Opening carrying amount × depreciation rate | £10,000 × 20% = £2,000 in year 1 |
| Carrying amount | Cost − accumulated depreciation − impairment | £3,000 − £50 = £2,950 |
| Impairment | A separate reduction when the asset's value is impaired | An unexpected loss of recoverable benefits |

Depreciation allocates an asset's depreciable cost across the periods using its benefits. Buying the machine is the cash outflow; depreciation later is a non-cash expense. It does not create a cash fund to replace the machine.

For reducing balance, year 2 starts from £8,000, so depreciation is £1,600. If cost C, positive residual value R and life n are given, a constant rate reaching R is **d = 1 − (R/C)^(1/n)**. A zero residual value cannot be reached exactly in finite time with a rate strictly below 100%; follow any final-year adjustment specified.

If an asset is sold, compare proceeds with its carrying amount to calculate the disposal gain or loss. The investing cash inflow is the proceeds, not just that gain.

For a constant reducing-balance fraction $d$ applied for $n$ years without other adjustments:

$$
BV_t=C(1-d)^t,\qquad d=1-\left(\frac{R}{C}\right)^{1/n}.
$$

$C$ is cost, $R>0$ residual value and $BV_t$ closing carrying amount. Use $d=0.20$ for 20%; do not substitute 20 into $1-d$. Record depreciation with a debit to expense and credit to accumulated depreciation. Record a disposal by removing both cost and accumulated depreciation; the difference between proceeds and net carrying amount is a gain/loss.

### 3.6 FIFO, weighted average and LIFO

Assume opening stock is zero, then buy 10 units at £5 and 10 at £7. Sell 12 units **after both purchases**; 8 remain.

| Cost-flow method | Cost of the 12 units sold | Closing inventory |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FIFO: oldest costs leave first | 10 × £5 + 2 × £7 = **£64** | 8 × £7 = **£56** |
| Weighted average | Average £120 ÷ 20 = £6; 12 × £6 = **£72** | 8 × £6 = **£48** |
| LIFO: newest costs leave first | 10 × £7 + 2 × £5 = **£80** | 8 × £5 = **£40** |

Each row satisfies **£120 available cost = cost of sales + closing inventory**. With rising purchase prices, FIFO produces lower cost of sales and higher closing inventory than LIFO in this example. The sales revenue is unchanged, so the expense difference changes profit.

For moving weighted average, recalculate average cost after each purchase; a period-end average can differ when sales occur between purchases. Distinguish cost-flow assumptions from the physical movement of goods. Chapter 3 discusses external-reporting restrictions, while Chapter 10's internal project exercise explicitly requests LIFO; use the method required by the exercise.

For the course's inventory valuation exercises, compare cost with net realisable value: **expected selling price − selling/completion costs still needed**. Use the lower value when required. A receivable that becomes irrecoverable similarly requires a loss and a reduction of the asset; follow any allowance information provided.

### 3.7 Revenue over time and receivable losses

When an exercise measures performance over time by cost-based progress, progress is **cost incurred to date ÷ total expected cost**. Cumulative revenue is contract price × progress; current-period revenue is cumulative recognised revenue less revenue already recognised. This measure is appropriate only when costs faithfully reflect the specified progress; it is not permission to recognise revenue whenever cash is received.

For a teaching contract priced at £100,000 with expected cost £80,000, £20,000 cost to date implies 25% progress and £25,000 cumulative revenue. If £10,000 revenue was recognised earlier, recognise £15,000 this period. Revise estimates when the facts change.

An identified irrecoverable customer balance reduces receivables and creates an expense if it has not already been provided for. With a receivables allowance, distinguish the write-off against that allowance from the period's expense for changing the allowance. A write-off and an increase in the allowance are not automatically two expenses for the same loss. For course exercises without an allowance, use the direct loss approach shown in the supplied material.

## DEB Double-entry bookkeeping

**Tasks beside the method:** [Open this chapter’s tasks + hints](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/Tasks/Home%20and%20tutoring) · [Reading, home and tutoring routes](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/Practice).

### DEB.1 Which side increases an account?

| Account type | Increase | Decrease |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Asset | Debit | Credit |
| Expense | Debit | Credit |
| Owner drawings / distributions account | Debit | Credit |
| Liability | Credit | Debit |
| Equity / owner capital | Credit | Debit |
| Revenue | Credit | Debit |

**Total debits must equal total credits for each entry.** A transaction can involve more than two accounts. Debit does not always mean an increase: a debit reduces a liability. A credit to the cash asset account means cash decreased.

Expenses normally have debit balances because they reduce the profit that will ultimately increase equity. Revenue normally has a credit balance because it increases that profit. This connects the bookkeeping rules to the accounting equation.

### DEB.2 A connected example: from transactions to statements

Assume a new business, one reporting month, no tax, no opening balances, no owner withdrawals and no other transactions. Equipment depreciation is £50 for the month. Rent of £900 covers three equal months beginning this month.

| Event | Debit | Credit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Owner contributes £10,000 to the bank | Bank 10,000 | Owner capital 10,000 |
| Buy equipment for £3,000 cash | Equipment 3,000 | Bank 3,000 |
| Buy £2,000 inventory on credit | Inventory 2,000 | Trade payables 2,000 |
| Sell goods for £2,000 on credit | Trade receivables 2,000 | Sales revenue 2,000 |
| Record the £1,200 cost of those goods | Cost of sales 1,200 | Inventory 1,200 |
| Collect £1,500 from the customer | Bank 1,500 | Trade receivables 1,500 |
| Pay the supplier £500 | Trade payables 500 | Bank 500 |
| Pay three months' rent, £900 | Prepaid rent 900 | Bank 900 |
| Recognise this month's rent, £300 | Rent expense 300 | Prepaid rent 300 |
| Recognise equipment depreciation, £50 | Depreciation expense 50 | Accumulated depreciation 50 |

The credit sale needs two entries: one records what the customer owes and the revenue earned; the other moves the sold goods' cost from inventory into an expense. This example uses continuous inventory records. If an exercise uses a purchases account and period-end inventory calculation, follow that system consistently.

### DEB.3 Balances, trial balance and statements

For an asset such as bank, closing balance = opening balance + receipts − payments. Here, **£10,000 − £3,000 + £1,500 − £500 − £900 = £7,100**. Receivables are £2,000 − £1,500 = £500; payables are £2,000 − £500 = £1,500.

| Adjusted trial balance | Debit £ | Credit £ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bank | 7,100 | |
| Equipment at cost | 3,000 | |
| Inventory | 800 | |
| Trade receivables | 500 | |
| Prepaid rent | 600 | |
| Cost of sales | 1,200 | |
| Rent expense | 300 | |
| Depreciation expense | 50 | |
| Owner capital | | 10,000 |
| Trade payables | | 1,500 |
| Sales revenue | | 2,000 |
| Accumulated depreciation | | 50 |
| **Total** | **13,550** | **13,550** |

Use revenue and expense accounts to prepare the income statement. The resulting £450 profit joins owner capital in equity; the remaining asset, liability and equity balances form the balance sheet. Accumulated depreciation is a **contra-asset**: it has a credit balance but reduces equipment rather than being a liability.

When balancing a T-account, **balance carried down** is the balancing figure needed to equalise the two sides. The **balance brought down** reopens the next period on the account's actual balance side. For bank here, the continuing balance is a debit of £7,100.

A trial balance catches unequal debits and credits. It can still balance after omitting a whole transaction, recording an equal wrong amount on both sides, or choosing the wrong accounts.

### DEB.4 Close the period without losing the connection

Adjustments belong before the final statements. To close the connected example's revenue, debit sales £2,000 and credit the income-summary account £2,000. Close the £1,550 total expenses with a debit to income summary and credits to the individual expense accounts. Income summary then has a £450 credit balance: debit it £450 and credit retained profit/equity £450. The temporary revenue and expense accounts reset; assets, liabilities and permanent equity balances carry forward.

If the course uses an income-statement account directly rather than an intermediate income-summary account, the same logic applies. Drawings close separately against equity and do not reduce operating profit.

The complete sequence is **identify → journal entry → ledger accounts → trial balance → adjustments → statements → closing entries**. Check the transaction's substance, not just equal totals. Accumulated depreciation reduces a particular asset; its credit balance does not turn it into a liability.

## 5 Measuring and reporting cash flows

**Tasks beside the method:** [Open this chapter’s tasks + hints](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/Tasks/Book%20chapter%205) · [Reading, home and tutoring routes](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/Practice).

### 5.1 Classify cash movements

| Category | Typical inflows | Typical outflows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Operating | Receipts from customers | Payments to suppliers and employees |
| Investing | Proceeds from selling equipment | Cash paid to acquire equipment |
| Financing | Owner contributions and new borrowings | Loan principal repayments and other financing payments |

Classification of interest, tax and distributions must follow the course or question's template. In particular, **the supplied Chapter 5 slide 13 deducts interest, taxation and dividends paid in its operating-cash-flow template**. Treat that as the course layout, rather than assuming every statement uses identical classifications.

**Closing cash = opening cash + operating cash flow + investing cash flow + financing cash flow.** Transfers between cash at hand and a bank account do not change their combined total.

Cash includes cash on hand and demand deposits. The course's cash-equivalent examples are short-term, highly liquid investments convertible into a known amount of cash with insignificant value risk. They are not all assets that could eventually be sold. In the supplied textbook convention, a qualifying demand overdraft integral to cash management may be included in the cash reconciliation; identify the question's treatment explicitly.

### 5.2 Direct method: follow receipts and payments

| Connected example | £ |
| --- | --- |
| Customer receipts | 1,500 |
| Payments to inventory supplier | (500) |
| Rent payment | (900) |
| **Net operating cash flow** | **100** |
| Equipment purchase: investing | (3,000) |
| Owner contribution: financing | 10,000 |
| **Net increase in cash / closing cash from zero** | **7,100** |

The £2,000 credit sale is not itself a cash receipt. Only £1,500 was collected. The £2,000 credit purchase is not itself a cash payment; £500 was paid.

### 5.3 Indirect method: bridge profit to operating cash

Start with the profit figure specified. Add back non-cash expenses, remove items belonging elsewhere, and adjust operating working capital. If starting with profit before tax in the course layout, add back interest expense before deducting actual interest paid separately.

| Change | Adjustment to profit | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Depreciation expense | Add back | Reduced profit without using cash this period |
| Inventory increases | Subtract | More cost remains tied up in unsold goods |
| Receivables increase | Subtract | Some earned revenue has not been collected |
| Prepayments increase | Subtract | Paid for benefits beyond this period |
| Operating payables/accruals increase | Add | Some costs or purchases have not yet been paid |

Reverse the working-capital signs for decreases. Exclude balances arising from financing or equipment purchases from an operating-working-capital adjustment.

For the example: **£450 profit + £50 depreciation − £800 inventory − £500 receivables − £600 prepayment + £1,500 trade payables = £100 operating cash flow.** This agrees with the direct method, despite profit being £450.

**Memory cue:** more operating assets generally tie up cash; more operating liabilities generally defer cash payments. A non-cash purchase of equipment on credit is not a cash outflow until payment occurs.

![cash-bridge](./static-data/vault-assets/EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/assets/cash-bridge.svg)

*The indirect bridge reaches the same £100 operating cash flow as the receipts-and-payments method in the connected example. Intermediate running totals may be negative; they are bridge arithmetic, not bank balances.*

### 5.3A Cash flow statement recipe — indirect method

**Purpose:** Explain how cash changed during the year. Use the income statement for that year, the opening and closing statements of financial position, and the question's notes. Figures in the income statement are for the period; balance-sheet figures are balances at a date.

**Complete fill-in template:** Use this from top to bottom. It follows the Chapter 5 home-assignment solution's indirect-method presentation. Include only lines relevant to the question; classification of interest and dividends can vary.

```text
STATEMENT OF CASH FLOWS FOR THE YEAR ENDED [DATE]       £ / £m

1. OPERATING ACTIVITIES
Profit before tax                                  ___
Add back depreciation                              +___
Add back interest expense                          +___
Adjust for inventory change                        +/−___
Adjust for trade receivables change                +/−___
Adjust for trade payables change                   +/−___
                                                  ------
Cash generated from operations                     ___
Less interest paid                                 −___
Less tax paid                                      −___
Less dividends paid                                −___
                                                  ------
Net cash from operating activities                 ___

2. INVESTING ACTIVITIES
Purchase of non-current assets                     −___
Proceeds from sale of non-current assets           +___
Other relevant investing cash flows                 +/−___
                                                  ------
Net cash from investing activities                 ___

3. FINANCING ACTIVITIES
Cash received from new loans                       +___
Cash received from issuing shares                  +___
Loan repayments                                    −___
Other relevant financing cash flows                 +/−___
                                                  ------
Net cash from financing activities                 ___

4. RECONCILIATION
Net cash from operating activities                 ___
Net cash from investing activities                 ___
Net cash from financing activities                 ___
                                                  ------
Net increase / decrease in cash                    ___
Opening cash and cash equivalents                   ___
                                                  ------
Closing cash and cash equivalents                  ___
```

- **Profit before tax:** take the current year's figure from the income statement. If the question starts from operating profit instead, check what it already includes; do not automatically add interest again.
- **Depreciation:** add back the current year's expense because it reduced profit without a current cash payment. If missing, a simple asset roll-forward is opening carrying value + additions − depreciation = closing carrying value, assuming no disposals or other changes.
- **Interest:** when starting from profit after interest, add back interest expense; then subtract interest actually paid in the separate payment line. They may differ. Tax paid can be found from opening tax payable + tax expense − closing tax payable, if there are no other movements. Use dividends actually paid, if stated.
- **Working capital signs:** inventory and receivables are operating assets: opening − closing. Operating payables are liabilities: closing − opening. Separate non-operating balances and adjust for write-downs or other non-cash movements where necessary.

**2. Investing activities:** show cash paid to buy and cash received from selling long-term assets. For example, purchases are outflows; disposal proceeds are inflows. Include only events relevant to the question.

**3. Financing activities:** show cash raised from or repaid to providers of finance, such as new loans, loan repayments and cash share issues. An increase in share capital is not necessarily a cash issue: check the notes. Interest and dividend classification can vary; follow the question or course template consistently.

**4. Check the cash balance:**

```text
Net operating cash + net investing cash + net financing cash = change in cash
Opening cash and cash equivalents + change in cash = closing cash and cash equivalents
```

Compare the result with the closing balance sheet. Where the question's treatment includes a qualifying bank overdraft in cash and cash equivalents, show that overdraft as a negative balance in the reconciliation; do not also count its change as financing cash flow. Otherwise follow the stated treatment.

**Study order:** set up the three sections; do operating adjustments; calculate investing and financing movements; reconcile opening to closing cash. Label the subtotal before interest, tax and dividends as *cash generated from operations* and the amount after them as *net operating cash flow*.

## 7 The relevance and behaviour of costs

**Tasks beside the method:** [Open this chapter’s tasks + hints](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/Tasks/Book%20chapter%207) · [Reading, home and tutoring routes](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/Practice).

### 7.1 Decide what belongs in the calculation

| Item | Include? | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Additional future cash cost | Yes | Caused by the choice |
| Avoidable future fixed cost | Yes | Changes when the action is taken |
| Sunk past cost | No | Already incurred and cannot be changed |
| Allocated fixed overhead unchanged by the choice | No | Reallocation does not change total cost |
| Opportunity cost | Yes | Value of the best alternative sacrificed |

**Fixed/variable** describes cost behaviour; **relevant/irrelevant** describes a particular decision. A new supervisor's fixed salary can be relevant to expansion. An existing unavoidable salary can be irrelevant to a one-off order.

### 7.2 Fixed, variable and mixed costs

| Cost type | Total behaviour | Per-unit behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fixed F | Constant within a relevant range | F/Q falls as output rises |
| Proportional variable cost | vQ rises with output | v stays constant |
| Mixed / semi-variable | Fixed element + variable element | F/Q + v |
| Stepped fixed cost | Jumps after a capacity threshold | Changes when the step is crossed |

Under the simple linear model: **total cost = F + vQ** and **profit = pQ − vQ − F = (p − v)Q − F**. These equations depend on their assumptions; a cost can become avoidable or change behaviour over a different time horizon.

![cost-behaviour](./static-data/vault-assets/EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/assets/cost-behaviour.svg)

*Distinguish total from per-unit behaviour. Fixed cost per unit falls with output; variable cost per unit stays constant in the simple linear model. Per-unit curves exclude Q = 0 because division by zero is undefined.*

### 7.3 Contribution and the break-even toolkit

$$\pi(Q)=(p-v)Q-F=cQ-F,\qquad Q_{BE}=\frac{F}{c}\quad(c>0).$$

| What you need | Formula | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit contribution c | p − v | Each sale's contribution towards fixed cost and then profit |
| Total contribution | cQ | Amount available to cover F |
| Contribution margin ratio | c/p | Contribution per £1 of sales |
| Break-even units | F/c | Units needed for zero profit, provided c is positive |
| Break-even sales revenue | F ÷ contribution margin ratio | Sales value needed for zero profit |
| Units for target profit P | (F + P)/c | Units needed to cover fixed cost and target profit |
| Margin of safety, units | Actual/planned Q − break-even Q | Volume cushion before a loss |
| Margin of safety, % | (Q − break-even Q)/Q × 100% | Cushion as a share of actual/planned sales |

Derive break-even rather than memorising blindly: zero profit means **cQ − F = 0**, therefore **cQ = F**, so **Q = F/c**. If units are indivisible, round required sales **up** to the next whole unit.

### 7.4 Worked example from the tutoring material

Motor Music sells radios for £60 each. Variable cost per radio is £20 materials + £14 labour + £12 other manufacturing + £3 selling = **£49**. Annual fixed costs are £80,000 + £60,000 = **£140,000**; planned annual sales are 20,000 radios.

Unit contribution = £60 − £49 = **£11**. Exact break-even volume = £140,000/£11 = **12,727.27 radios per year**; the minimum whole-unit sales level avoiding a loss is **12,728**. Theoretical break-even revenue = 12,727.27 × £60 = **£763,636.36**.

Planned contribution = 20,000 × £11 = £220,000, so planned profit = **£80,000**. Margin of safety using the unrounded threshold = 20,000 − 12,727.27 = **7,272.73 radios**, or **36.36%** of planned sales. Its sales value is **£436,363.64**. Keep the rounding convention visible.

![break-even](./static-data/vault-assets/EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/assets/break-even.svg)

*Motor Music: revenue £60Q intersects total cost £140,000 + £49Q at 12,727.27 radios. The plotted axes show radios and £000; whole-unit break-even is 12,728.*

### 7.5 Operating gearing and limitations

A business with more fixed cost and less variable cost can gain more profit from extra sales after fixed costs are covered, but also lose profit more quickly when demand falls. At a profitable activity level in this simple model, **degree of operating gearing = total contribution / operating profit**.

Break-even analysis assumes a relevant activity range, stable unit price and variable cost, fixed costs that do not change inside the range, and a stable sales mix for multiple products. Capacity limits, demand-dependent prices and stepped costs can invalidate a single straight-line answer. A multi-product break-even calculation needs an explicit sales-mix assumption.

### 7.6 Reusable decision patterns

| Decision | Calculation | Also check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Special order | Extra revenue − extra costs − opportunity cost | Spare capacity, displaced customers, future pricing |
| Make or buy | Relevant internal cost versus purchase cost plus associated costs | Quality, reliability, alternative use of capacity |
| Close or continue | Avoidable costs saved versus contribution lost | Costs that remain, exit costs, effects on other activities |
| Choose product mix | Contribution per unit of the scarce resource | Demand limits and available capacity |

Example: an extra order for 100 units brings £30 each and creates £18 variable cost each plus a £200 setup cost. With unused capacity and unchanged other costs, incremental profit = **100 × (£30 − £18) − £200 = £1,000**. If it displaces work earning £1,200 contribution, the opportunity cost changes the result to **−£200**.

### 7.7 A single scarce resource at fixed selling prices

| Product | Contribution per unit | Hours per unit | Contribution per hour |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | £30 | 3 | £10 |
| B | £24 | 2 | £12 |

With labour hours as the only binding constraint, prioritise B, subject to customer demand. Then allocate remaining hours to A. Ranking by contribution per **product** would choose A and misuse the scarce resource.

This ranking assumes constant incremental contributions. Multiple binding constraints or prices that fall with volume require a broader optimisation calculation.

Before ranking, test which resource is actually scarce: required resource = demand × resource per unit, summed over products. Compare this with each resource's availability. A resource with unused capacity has no scarcity premium in this model. With multiple binding limits, one contribution ranking can be insufficient; verify all constraints after allocating capacity.

### 7.8 Rebuild costs from two periods

With unchanged price, unit variable cost and fixed cost, $\Delta\pi=c\Delta Q$. Thus $c=(\pi_2-\pi_1)/(Q_2-Q_1)$, $p=R/Q$, $v=p-c$, and $F=cQ-\pi$.

The Chapter 7 home assignment reports April $Q=500$, revenue £25,000 and profit £10,000; May $Q=620$, revenue £31,000 and profit £14,000. Price is £50 in both. Contribution per unit is £4,000/120 = £33.3333; variable cost is £16.6667; fixed cost is £6,666.67. Break-even is **200 units**, with the unrounded values. A changed price or fixed-cost step would invalidate the two-period shortcut.

### 7.9 Equal profitability per scarce kilogram

In the same assignment, material costs £12/kg and is scarce. X has £30 unit variable cost and sells for £60, so its £30 contribution over 0.75kg gives **£40 contribution/kg**. Y uses 1kg and has £45 variable cost: equal profitability requires £40 contribution and a price of **£85**. Z uses 1.25kg and has £54 variable cost: it needs £50 contribution and a price of **£104**. Unchanged allocated fixed overhead is excluded. This is a calculation of the price needed to equalise resource returns, not proof that customers will accept it.

### 7.10 Opportunity cost with demand-dependent prices

The supplement gives p₁ = 2,100 − 10x₁ and p₂ = 1,050 − 20x₂, variable costs £100 and £50 per unit, and 720 available machine hours. Each unit uses 10 hours or 5 hours respectively.

Profit is **P = 2,000x₁ − 10x₁² + 1,000x₂ − 20x₂²**. Without the machine constraint, setting the two marginal profits to zero gives x₁ = 100 and x₂ = 25. They require 1,125 machine hours, exceeding 720; that apparent optimum is infeasible.

Introduce λ as the value of one additional hour. The constrained conditions are **2,000 − 20x₁ = 10λ**, **1,000 − 40x₂ = 5λ**, and **10x₁ + 5x₂ = 720**. The solution is **x₁ = 64, x₂ = 16, λ = £72 per hour**, producing profit **£97,920**. The raw-material constraint remains slack: 4 × 64 + 16 × 16 = 512 kg, below 2,000 kg available.

The economic interpretation is the important connection: product 1 sacrifices £720 of scarce machine capacity per unit, and product 2 sacrifices £360. Including those opportunity costs gives effective marginal costs £820 and £410. The shadow price applies locally around this optimum; do not assume the same £72 holds after a large capacity change.

![scarce-capacity](./static-data/vault-assets/EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/assets/scarce-capacity.svg)

*The unconstrained (100, 25) plan breaches machine capacity. The feasible optimum (64, 16) uses all 720 machine hours but only 512kg of the 2,000kg material supply. Profit contours are in £; the material boundary is also shown so both constraints can be checked.*

## 8 Full costing

**Tasks beside the method:** [Open this chapter’s tasks + hints](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/Tasks/Book%20chapter%208) · [Reading, home and tutoring routes](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/Practice).

### 8.1 Direct/indirect is a separate classification

**Direct costs** can be traced economically to the chosen cost object; **indirect costs** are shared and need allocation. The cost object might be one product, a job, a department or a customer.

| Example | Behaviour | Traceability to a product |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Materials used in each unit | Variable | Direct |
| Salary of a manager dedicated to one product | Fixed in the period | Direct to that product |
| Electricity serving several products | Can vary with activity | Indirect if not traced separately |
| Shared factory rent | Fixed in the range | Indirect |

For one homogeneous product, **full cost per unit = total relevant production cost for the period / units produced**, under the question's assumptions about completed output and inventory. A mixed product business generally needs a more specific allocation method.

### 8.2 Traditional overhead absorption

$$\text{Pool rate}=\frac{\text{pool overhead}}{\text{total base usage}},\qquad\text{job charge}=\text{rate}\times\text{job usage}.$$

| Step | Method | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Establish an overhead pool | Identify shared cost for a period/department | £60,000 overhead |
| Select an activity base | Choose a suitable service/use measure | 3,000 machine hours |
| Calculate absorption rate | Overhead / total activity | £20 per machine hour |
| Charge the job | Rate × job's usage | 4 hours × £20 = £80 |
| Derive full job cost | Direct costs + absorbed overhead | £70 materials + £50 labour + £80 = **£200** |

Use separate departmental rates when appropriate. Be consistent about the numerator and denominator: the overhead and activity must refer to the same pool and period. A budget-based rate need not allocate exactly the eventual actual overhead.

Allocation makes shared cost visible, but the allocated amount is not necessarily a cost that disappears if the product is discontinued. Return to Chapter 7 for that decision.

### 8.3 Activity-based costing (ABC)

ABC uses several activity pools and the drivers causing their resource use. **Pool rate = pool cost / total driver units; charge to a job = pool rate × driver units used by that job.** Sum the charges from all relevant pools, then add direct costs.

| Activity pool | Total cost / driver quantity | Rate | Job usage / charge |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Setups | £12,000 / 30 setups | £400 per setup | 2 setups → £800 |
| Order handling | £6,000 / 120 orders | £50 per order | 3 orders → £150 |
| **Allocated to this job** | | | **£950** |

£950 is a **job total**. If the job makes 100 units, it contributes £9.50 overhead per unit. Confusing a batch total with a unit amount is a frequent mistake.

In the lecture's storage example, 50,000 units of A use one week each and 25,000 units of B use four weeks each. Total driver use is **150,000 product-weeks**. £90,000/150,000 = **£0.60 per product-week**; storage overhead is £0.60 per A and £2.40 per B. Counting only units would miss B's greater storage use.

### 8.4 Mark-up and margin

| Question | Formula | Example with £80 cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Add a 25% mark-up on cost | Price = cost × (1 + mark-up) | £80 × 1.25 = **£100** |
| Obtain a 25% margin on selling price | Price = cost / (1 − margin) | £80 / 0.75 = **£106.67** |
| Margin implied by a 25% mark-up | Mark-up / (1 + mark-up) | 0.25/1.25 = **20%** |

Always identify the percentage's base. A £20 profit on £80 cost is a 25% mark-up, but that £20 is only 20% of the £100 selling price.

### 8.5 Why cost-plus pricing can fail

The supplement uses **C(Q) = 100Q + 2,000** and **p = 200 − Q**. Therefore revenue is 200Q − Q² and profit is **100Q − Q² − 2,000**. Marginal profit is 100 − 2Q, giving **Q = 50**, **p = £150**, and profit **£500** at the interior maximum.

A mechanical 20% mark-up on the full unit cost at Q = 50 gives (100 + 2,000/50) × 1.20 = **£168**. At that price demand falls to 32 units. Recalculating unit cost using 32 gives £162.50 and a new price of £195, reducing demand to 5 units. Repeating gives £600, with zero demand under the example.

The connection is circular: a higher price reduces demand; lower volume spreads fixed cost over fewer units; the calculated unit cost rises again. A cost-plus price needs a demand and capacity check. The profit-maximising example uses marginal revenue equal to marginal cost.

![cost-plus](./static-data/vault-assets/EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/assets/cost-plus.svg)

*The marginal-revenue and marginal-cost intersection gives Q = 50 and p = £150. The corresponding profit is £500. Full unit cost depends on Q, so a mark-up calculation needs a demand check.*

### 8.6 Departmental rates, batch costs and absorption checks

A **cost unit** is the unit whose cost is measured; a **cost centre** is a department, function or location where costs are collected. A batch may be one job: divide total batch cost by its unit count only after assigning its full job cost.

For the lecture's £20,000 overhead pool, £8,000 is machine-related over 1,000 machine hours and £12,000 labour-related over 1,600 labour hours. The rates are £8/machine hour and £7.50/labour hour. Job 1 uses 700 machine and 800 labour hours: overhead is **£11,600**. Job 2 uses 300 machine and 800 labour hours: **£8,400**. The allocation totals £20,000. This better reflects the different usage than charging both jobs the same amount from their identical labour hours.

In the Chapter 8 Patel assignment, total cost £1,520,000 less £600,000 direct labour and £200,000 direct materials leaves **£720,000 overhead**. The labour-hour rate is **£7.20** (100,000 hours); the machine-hour rate is **£8** (90,000 hours). Direct labour costs £6/hour. Order 101's £5,000 materials and 4,000 labour hours therefore give £29,000 direct cost. Full cost is **£57,800** using labour hours or **£44,200** using its 1,900 machine hours. Neither is automatically the uniquely “true” cost; discuss which activities drive the shared costs and whether separate pools would improve the estimate.

With a predetermined budget rate, **absorbed overhead = rate × actual activity**. Under-absorption is actual overhead minus absorbed overhead when that difference is positive; over-absorption is the reverse. For £60,000 actual overhead and only 2,800 hours charged at £20, absorption is £56,000 and under-absorption £4,000. Reconcile before treating an allocated product cost as an actual total.

ABC can improve attribution when products consume support activities differently. It also costs time and data collection, and a poorly chosen driver can still mislead. Full-cost information helps pricing, control, efficiency comparisons and profit measurement. For a short-run special order or closure, return to relevant costs: an allocated share need not be avoidable.

## 10 Making capital investment decisions

**Tasks beside the method:** [Open this chapter’s tasks + hints](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/Tasks/Book%20chapter%2010) · [Reading, home and tutoring routes](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/Practice).

### 10.1 Choose the correct measure

| Method | Uses | Basic decision rule | Main limitation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Accounting rate of return, ARR | Average accounting profit / average investment | Meet the required ARR | Ignores timing and depends on accounting measures |
| Payback period | Undiscounted net cash flows | Recover the investment within the allowed time | Ignores later flows and time value |
| Net present value, NPV | All relevant dated cash flows, discounted | Accept a positive-NPV independent project | Depends on cash-flow forecasts and discount rate |
| Internal rate of return, IRR | Rate making NPV zero | For conventional flows, exceed required return | Can mis-rank projects or produce multiple/no useful roots |

At NPV = 0, a project earns exactly the required return under its assumptions. For mutually exclusive feasible alternatives, compare value created using consistent assumptions and the appropriate NPV analysis; a larger percentage IRR need not create more wealth.

### 10.2 ARR: profit after depreciation

**ARR = average annual operating profit / average investment × 100%.** In the lecture's simple straight-line example, average investment = **(initial cost + residual value)/2**. Include other tied-up capital if the question requires it.

The lecture uses initial machine cost 100, residual value 20 and five annual pre-depreciation operating amounts of 20, 40, 60, 60 and 20. Average before depreciation = 40; annual depreciation = (100 − 20)/5 = 16; average profit = **24**. Average investment = (100 + 20)/2 = **60**, so **ARR = 40%**.

The figures are in thousands in the lecture. The common scale cancels from the percentage. Dividing 24 by the initial 100 instead would answer a different ARR convention.

### 10.3 Payback: accumulate cash

Using that lecture example, the initial 100 outflow is recovered through inflows of 20, 40, 60, 60 and 20, plus residual proceeds 20 in year 5. After year 2, 40 remains unrecovered. If year 3's 60 arrives evenly, **payback = 2 + 40/60 = 2.67 years**.

If the money arrives only at each year-end, recovery occurs at the end of year 3; the fractional-year calculation needs the even-flow assumption. Payback says how quickly the initial outlay returns, rather than measuring all value created.

### 10.4 Time value of money and NPV

$$NPV=CF_0+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{CF_t}{(1+r)^t},\qquad CF_0=-I_0.$$

Future cash flows are dated at year-end unless the question says otherwise. $I_0$ is the initial cash investment, entered once.

| Need | Formula | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Future value of one sum | $FV=PV(1+r)^t$ | £100 × 1.10² = £121 |
| Present value of a future sum | $CF_t/(1+r)^t$ | £121 / 1.10² = £100 |
| Net present value | $CF_0+\sum_{t=1}^{T}CF_t/(1+r)^t$ | Include the initial outflow with a negative sign |

Discounting expresses money at different dates in comparable present-value terms. The discount rate represents the required return/opportunity cost for the relevant risk. A larger discount rate reduces the present value of a given positive future receipt.

**Small worked example:** pay £1,000 now; receive £600 at each of the next two year-ends; r = 10%. NPV = −1,000 + 600/1.10 + 600/1.10² = −1,000 + 545.45 + 495.87 = **£41.32**. This is value above the required 10% return; the £1,200 undiscounted receipts are not the NPV.

### 10.5 IRR: the break-even discount rate

$$0=CF_0+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{CF_t}{(1+IRR)^t}.$$

IRR solves the discounted cash-flow equation above. For the two-year example above, IRR is approximately **13.07%**. At a required return of 10%, its positive NPV and higher IRR give the same acceptance signal for this conventional project.

An approximate interpolation is **IRR ≈ r_low + [NPV_low/(NPV_low − NPV_high)] × (r_high − r_low)**, using a positive NPV at the lower rate and a negative NPV at the higher rate. It is an approximation because NPV is generally curved in r. A financial calculator or spreadsheet solver can find the root more accurately.

Cash flows changing sign more than once can produce multiple IRRs. With mutually exclusive projects, scale and timing differences can make IRR and NPV rankings disagree. State the actual cash-flow pattern and prefer the analysis of value created.

### 10.6 Build the investment cash-flow timeline

Include additional future operating cash flows, opportunity costs, initial capital expenditure, later relevant capital spending, disposal receipts, working-capital investments/releases, and tax effects **when specified**. Exclude sunk costs and unchanged overhead allocations.

Depreciation is not a cash payment, although it can affect tax when a tax mechanism is given. In the course's project cash-flow approach, financing cost is already reflected in the discount rate, so do not also subtract loan interest as a project operating cash flow. An equity-cash-flow question would need its own consistent financing treatment.

Investment in inventory or receivables can tie up additional cash at the start or during the project. Release it at the end only to the extent recovery is justified by the question. Use r as a decimal, match rate and period, and keep the initial outlay at t = 0 undiscounted.

![npv-profile](./static-data/vault-assets/EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/assets/npv-profile.svg)

*For cash flows −£1,000, +£600, +£600, NPV falls as the discount rate rises. The zero crossing is the IRR, about 13.07%; at 10% NPV is +£41.32. This monotonic picture uses a conventional cash-flow pattern.*

The annuity shortcut for the same receipt $a$ at each of $T$ year-ends is $PV=a[1-(1+r)^{-T}]/r$ for $r\ne0$. At $r=0$, use $aT$. It does not apply unchanged to irregular amounts, payments at the beginning of years or a separate terminal value.

### 10.7 Calculate the capital charge

$$RI_t=NI_t-r\,OA_{t-1}.$$

**Residual income = operating profit − required rate × opening operating assets.** In the lecture's no-interest, no-tax exercise, the profit measure is described as net income. Use a profit measure and capital base consistent with the required return.

Operating assets tied to a project can include equipment carrying amount, inventory and receivables, net of relevant operating liabilities. In the lecture's simplified exercise, follow its definition of operating assets and its cash/expense timing.

With opening operating assets £1,000, profit £100 and required return 10%, the charge is £100 and residual income is **zero**. The project has accounting profit but only earns the required return. With the same capital and £150 profit, residual income is **£50**.

### 10.8 Why discounted residual income can equal NPV

With consistent accrual accounting, **closing operating assets = opening operating assets + profit − free cash flow**, with investment and working-capital flows included consistently. Rearranging gives $FCF_t=NI_t-(OA_t-OA_{t-1})$.

Substituting profit = RI + r × opening operating assets and discounting causes the intermediate operating-asset amounts to cancel. For an initial investment OA₀ and terminal operating assets of zero, this gives **project NPV = Σ[RI_t/(1 + r)^t], t = 1…T**. This is the course's Lücke–Preinreich connection. If terminal operating assets remain, include their consistent terminal treatment; the simple equality cannot be used while silently leaving capital unrecovered.

The **existing operating-asset value** is a separate quantity: under the same terminal assumptions it is **OA₀ + present value of future RI**. Do not add OA₀ again when the question asks for NPV after the initial investment.

### 10.9 Worked reconciliation using the small investment project

Assume the £1,000 investment depreciates straight line over two years to zero, no tax, no working capital, and £600 operating cash inflow at each year-end. Annual depreciation is £500, so annual profit is £100.

| Year | Opening operating assets | Profit | 10% capital charge | Residual income | PV of RI |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | £1,000 | £100 | £100 | £0 | £0 |
| 2 | £500 | £100 | £50 | £50 | £41.32 |
| **Total** | | | | | **£41.32** |

The present value of RI equals the **£41.32 NPV** calculated from cash flows in Chapter 10. The discounted profits alone equal £173.55; that number fails to charge for the capital tied up in the project.

### 10.10 The full course capstone: what must be kept separate

The Chapter 10 capstone combines credit sales, production, LIFO inventory and a £50,000 machine. Sales are earned in one year but some receipts occur later; production cost is paid when produced but expensed when units sell; depreciation allocates the machine's cost over five years.

Its verified results are **NPV £11,201.73**, **PV of net income £25,651.69** and **PV of residual income £11,201.73**. Total undiscounted profit and total project cash flow both equal £35,500 after terminal balances are cleared. Equality of undiscounted totals does not imply equality of discounted profit and cash flow. See [the full period-by-period reconciliation](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3430-Obsidian/EXC3430-support/Worked%20Examples%23Course%20capstone).

For $t\ge1$, the capital roll-forward is $OA_t=OA_{t-1}+NI_t-FCF_t$. Combining it with $RI_t=NI_t-rOA_{t-1}$ gives:

$$
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{FCF_t}{(1+r)^t}
=OA_0+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{RI_t}{(1+r)^t}
-\frac{OA_T}{(1+r)^T}.
$$

If $CF_0=-OA_0$ and terminal capital is fully realised so $OA_T=0$, project NPV is the discounted RI sum. If capital remains, a terminal adjustment is required. This assumes consistent cash flows, accrual accounting, capital bases and discount rates. Evaluating the full discounted RI stream can align value measurement with NPV; it does not guarantee good incentives from a single year's bonus or a manipulated accounting estimate.
